newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel approves controversial Jerusalem project.
newsitem.headline: Israel approves controversial Jerusalem project.

text.p: Israel approved on Wednesday the building of new Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem despite warnings the project could unleash a wave of Palestinian violence.

Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh told reporters a ministerial committee on Jerusalem approved the construction of 6,500 homes for Jews, with 2,500 to be built in the first stage. Another 3,000 housing units would be built for Arabs.
The homes will be built at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel, a tree-covered hill taken by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war. The site is between Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
Palestinians warned the project could touch off anti-Israeli violence in the West Bank and Gaza reminiscent of clashes in September in which 61 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed.
But Israeli security officials told the committee they believed the Palestinians would bottle their anger, at least until bulldozers began work, Israel Radio reported.
"After the minister of labour and welfare signs the plans, we can start immediately work on the infrastructure of Har Homa," Naveh said, without citing a specific date.
The United States has expressed its concern about the project, calling on Israel and the PLO to avoid violence.

"The struggle for Jerusalem has begun," Police Minister Avigdor Kahalani said before the ministerial session. "When we decide today, we will make it clear once and for all that Jerusalem is the capital of the Jewish people."
Palestinians see the project it as an attempt to pre-empt a decision on the final status of Jerusalem, which is supposed to be decided in future talks that must be completed by 1999.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said anyone who resorted to violence over the project would be making a "grave mistake", his spokesman said.
In a bid to blunt Arab anger, Netanyahu spoke by telephone with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak before the meeting about the project.

"Prime Minister Netanyahu...(told Mubarak that Israel) intends to build about 2,000 housing units for Jews in the Har Homa neighbourhood on land which is largely private and under Jewish ownership," a spokesman said, referring to the project's first stage.
Palestinians and Israeli leftists have warned the plan could ignite Arab rage like the September clashes after Netanyahu opened a tunnel entrance near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.
"There are scenarios that say there will be riots and possibly the opening of fire -- we are not naive," Kahalani told Army radio.
Major-General Uzi Dayan, commander of Israeli forces in the West Bank, said the army had not sent reinforcements to the area but had "concentrated troops in the necessary places".
Israeli security sources said an army plan in the event of clashes called for deploying tanks and snipers in areas of the West Bank and Gaza still under military occupation.
